title: Construction Damaging a Neighbor's House: Who Pays? (2026)
desc: Construction cracks a neighbor's house: who pays, owner or contractor, what is covered, limitation period and fines under the Civil Code and Decree 339/2026.
summary: The liability of homeowners and contractors when construction causes an adjoining house to settle or crack: civil compensation, administrative fines, and how to resolve disputes with the neighbor.
body: p

Digging foundations, driving piles, and building basements are when a neighbor's house is most likely to settle or crack. This article summarizes the responsibility of homeowners and contractors under the Civil Code 2015, the Construction Law 2025, and Decree 339/2026/ND-CP.
h2
1. The duty to keep adjoining houses safe
ul

When building, the owner must comply with construction law, ensure safety, and must not infringe the lawful rights and interests of owners of adjoining and surrounding real estate (Article 174 of the Civil Code).
Construction must ensure the safety of underground works and adjoining buildings, with measures to limit damage if an incident occurs (Clause 2, Article 50 of the Construction Law 2025).

The owner of a detached house who organizes construction and supervision is responsible for safety toward neighboring buildings (Point b, Clause 3, Article 10 of Decree 207/2026/ND-CP). The permit application must also include a written undertaking to ensure safety for adjoining buildings (Article 60 of Decree 217/2026/ND-CP).
h2
2. Who must pay compensation?
ul
A person who infringes another person's property and causes damage must pay compensation (Article 584 of the Civil Code).
The owner, possessor, or manager of a house or building must compensate for damage caused by it; if the builder is at fault, the builder must be jointly liable (Article 605).
Where several people cause damage together, they are jointly liable; each person's share corresponds to their degree of fault, or is divided equally if it cannot be determined (Article 587).

A construction contractor must compensate for damage when its work does not meet quality requirements and for other violations it causes (Point k, Clause 2, Article 61 of the Construction Law). If the contractor is a company, the company compensates for damage caused by its personnel while carrying out assigned work (Article 597).
p

In practice, neighbors often demand compensation from the homeowner; the homeowner can in turn require the at-fault contractor to take responsibility under the contract. The construction contract should therefore state clearly who is responsible for the safety of adjoining houses.
h2
3. What is compensated?
p
Under Article 589 and Article 585 of the Civil Code, compensation covers:
ul
Property that is damaged or lost (the cost of repairing walls, floors, and structures that have settled or cracked, etc.);
Benefits tied to the use of property that is lost or reduced (for example, being unable to rent out the house);
Reasonable costs to prevent, limit, and remedy the damage.
p

Actual damage must be compensated in full and promptly; the parties may agree on the amount and form of compensation. If the injured party does not take reasonable measures to limit their own damage, they are not compensated for that part.
h2
4. Administrative fines also apply
ul

A homeowner who builds contrary to the approved method and fails to ensure safety, causing settlement, cracking, or damage to, or risk of collapse of, a neighboring building (without harm to people): VND 30–40 million for a detached house (Clause 5, Article 25).
A contractor that violates quality management rules and causes settlement or cracking in a neighboring building: VND 30–40 million for a detached house (Clause 2, Article 26).
These are the amounts for organizations; individuals are fined half (Clause 4, Article 5). Paying a fine does not replace the obligation to compensate the neighbor.
h2
5. What should homeowners and neighbors do?
ol
Before starting work: together with the neighbor, take photos and videos and prepare a record of the condition of the adjoining house (old cracks, tilt).
Require the contractor to prepare a construction method, shoring, and monitoring when building foundations and basements.
When settlement or cracks are found: stop the related work, prepare a record, and negotiate the compensation in writing.

If no agreement is reached: report to the commune- or ward-level People's Committee or file a lawsuit in court. The limitation period for suing for compensation is 3 years from the date the person knew their rights were infringed (Article 588).
p
See also the conditions before breaking ground in Conditions for starting construction of a house 2026.
note

This article is a summary for reference only and does not replace legal documents. The specific compensation depends on the actual damage and each party's fault; in a dispute, it is advisable to commission an expert assessment and seek advice from a lawyer.
